context: Eight learners each count the number of sweets they have; the first count listed is far from all the others.

params.why: the typical values must be spread enough that the new range is clearly different from the one with the outlier

stem: A group of $8$ learners count the number of sweets they each have. This is the data they collect: $\left\{ {=out}, {=s[0]}, {=s[1]}, {=s[2]}, {=s[3]}, {=s[4]}, {=s[5]}, {=s[6]} \right\}$ The first value, ${=out}$, is not typical of the other values. What happens to the range of the data set if the first value is removed?
solution: Put the data set in order, from the smallest value to the largest: $\left\{ {=fs[0]}, {=fs[1]}, {=fs[2]}, {=fs[3]}, {=fs[4]}, {=fs[5]}, {=fs[6]}, {=fs[7]} \right\}$
The maximum value is ${=mx}$ and the minimum value is ${=mn}$, so the range is ${=mx} - {=mn} = {=rng1}$.
Remove the first value, ${=out}$. The data set that is left, in order, is $\left\{ {=cs[0]}, {=cs[1]}, {=cs[2]}, {=cs[3]}, {=cs[4]}, {=cs[5]}, {=cs[6]} \right\}$
The new maximum value is ${=cmax}$ and the new minimum value is ${=cmin}$, so the new range is ${=cmax} - {=cmin} = {=rng2}$.

The range decreases from ${=rng1}$ to ${=rng2}$. The value ${=out}$ is not typical of the other values: it is an outlier, and it has a big influence on the range because the range depends only on the largest and the smallest value.

distractors.text: The range stays at ${=rng1}$, because only one of the values is removed.
The range decreases by $1$, from ${=rng1}$ to ${=rng1 - 1}$.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Adds 1 to the difference when finding the range
proposed_misconceptions.description: Finds the range as maximum - minimum + 1, counting the whole numbers from the smallest value to the largest (both ends included) instead of subtracting the minimum from the maximum.

notes: Mirrors the book's we10 exactly in shape: the FIRST value listed is the outlier and the question is what happens to the range when it is removed. Here the answer is chosen from statements, which is a natural classification of the effect (unchanged or decreases, and to what). The outlier is the unique extreme (core values lie in a window of width 8, outlier is 11 to 15 beyond the nearest core extreme), low or high by 'side'. Distractor 1 is the catalogued misconception (range unchanged). Distractor 2 is the inclusive-counting slip applied consistently to both ranges (R+1, R2+1), so a student who adds 1 finds their own answer listed. Distractor 3 (decreases by 1) has no named error, so it carries null; it is always false because gap >= 11. The four option texts are always distinct and only the correct one states both true ranges. Sweets cannot be negative: base >= 16 and gap <= 15 keep a low outlier at 1 or more. Stem has holes that differ per instance, so distinct_by_choices is not set.
